evals.prompt: I'm giving a 25-minute talk at Cascadia Infra Days on November 12 about our CLI, Riftline, and the demo gets 8 minutes of that. Last year at a different event the whole thing died because the venue Wi-Fi couldn't reach our staging cluster and I stood there typing for four minutes in front of 300 people. I have about two full days I can put into this before the event, and I'll be giving basically this same talk at four more events through next spring. The demo has to convince people Riftline can reindex a 2-million-row table while writes keep landing. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: A demo runbook: the claim in one sentence, a tier-2 fully-local recommendation justified by re-use across five events, segments under ~90s each with independent restore points, a one-command idempotent reset, a tier-3 recorded fallback, and a rehearsal gate with three clean cold runs and an offline run.
expectations: States the demo's claim as a single sentence about reindexing while concurrent writes keep landing
Recommends the fully-local, offline live-execution tier (tier 2) rather than a recorded screencast or a live run against the staging cluster
Cites the re-use across five events as the reason the cost of building a local stack is amortized and that tier is promoted
Names the standing fallback as exactly one row down the ladder, a recorded screencast of the same segments, rather than jumping to screenshots
Cuts the demo into segments each budgeted under roughly 90 seconds
Names each segment by what it proves rather than by the commands it types
Gives every segment its own named restore point (git tag, image tag, database dump, seeded tenant or equivalent)
States that no segment may depend on a previous segment's live output
Specifies a single idempotent reset command and requires it to be rehearsed from a cold machine, not from one that has already run the demo
Requires at least one full rehearsal run with the network disconnected
Requires three consecutive clean cold runs before the demo is considered ready
Requires the measured demo time to come in under half the 8 minutes allowed
Does not offer additional rehearsal repetitions as the fix for the previous event's failure

evals.prompt: Honest question. I have to show our new Postgres query planner visualizer at a 300-person keynote in nine days and I am terrified. The demo is basically: paste a slow query, watch the visualizer draw the plan tree, click one node, see the index suggestion. That's it. My co-founder says just take screenshots and talk over them so nothing can break. I have about six hours total to spend on demo prep. Which way do I go?
evals.expected_output: A settled fidelity decision: a recorded screencast played inside the deck with live narration, with annotated screenshots as the standing fallback, the screenshots-only plan rejected on efficiency grounds, and the live-typing tiers ruled out by the six-hour prep budget.
expectations: Recommends a recorded screencast played inside the deck as the primary plan
Explicitly rejects annotated screenshots as the primary plan
Explains that screenshots buy near-zero proof for near-zero effort, so the cheapest option is not the most efficient one
Requires the narration to stay live over the recorded screen
Warns that pre-recording the commentary as well turns the session into a video and disengages the audience
Names annotated screenshots or a diagram as the standing fallback below the recorded screencast
Rules out the live-typing tiers because six hours of prep cannot make them safe
Presents two or three candidate tiers with their trade-offs before recommending one
Notes that the recording has to be re-recorded whenever the product UI moves
Does not present the tier ladder to the user as a published or industry-standard framework
Orders the options by value returned per unit of effort rather than by cost alone
Settles the live-versus-recorded decision without producing an unrequested slide-by-slide talk outline

evals.prompt: We're announcing Vaneer Sync at our user conference on the 3rd and the feature is under embargo until the keynote starts. Legal already told me nothing about it can leave the building before then, which includes any recording or screenshot leaving my laptop. I need to show it doing a two-way sync against a real-looking CRM in about six minutes on stage. I've got three weeks and an engineer who can help. How should I build this?
evals.expected_output: A tier-2 fully-local design: the recorded and screenshot tiers deleted and named as deleted because the embargoed UI cannot leave the room, seeded synthetic CRM fixtures that trigger no review, a fallback that keeps the material inside the room, a full-screen pre-flight pass and per-segment restore points.
expectations: Deletes the recorded-screencast and annotated-screenshot tiers from the options because the embargoed UI cannot leave the room
Says explicitly which tiers were deleted and why, rather than silently leaving them available as fallbacks
Recommends the fully-local, offline live-execution tier
Explains that seeded local fixtures trigger no legal or comms review, which is what promotes that tier under an embargo
Does not offer a recorded clip or a screenshot as the fallback for any segment
Proposes a fallback that keeps the embargoed material inside the room, such as a reduced local path, a pre-seeded end state, or a diagram
Specifies synthetic CRM fixtures rather than anonymised records from a real customer
Explains that anonymising real data leaves re-identifiable traces such as email domains, URLs, ticket references, codenames or a colleague's name
Requires the embargoed feature to be flagged off anywhere outside the demo path, and every screen that will be shown to be checked first
Requires a pre-flight pass over error states, empty states, dropdowns and autocomplete, not only the screens the happy path visits
Requires a dedicated demo repository with clean or no history rather than the team's working repo
Requires human redundancy, a colleague holding a clone of everything on a working machine, for the dead-laptop case
Requires each segment to be enterable from its own restore point without running the segments before it

evals.prompt: Our pitch is that Kelvinsort dedupes a 10M-record contact list in under 30 seconds. On my laptop it takes about 4 minutes because the machine is slow, and roughly one run in five the progress bar stalls at 80% for no reason I can find. I'm on at a partner summit in two weeks in front of maybe 60 buyers. I was thinking of just putting a timer-driven progress bar in the demo build so it always lands at 28 seconds, and filtering the one weird record class out of the verification count so the totals match. Can you help me put that together?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build either fake, both named as faking the output rather than hardening the setup, the claim narrowed to what the system genuinely does today, and a list of legitimate hardening moves plus a designed fallback for the intermittent stall.
expectations: Refuses to build the timer-driven progress bar
Refuses to filter the anomalous record class out of the verification count
Names both requests as faking the output rather than hardening the setup
States the rule that hardening applies to the setup and never to the output
Applies the test of whether the speaker could answer "is that real?" with yes and prove it on the spot
Warns that being caught faking costs exactly the credibility the live demo was buying
Recommends narrowing the claim to something the system does today, such as the dataset size or hardware on which the 30-second figure actually holds
Offers legitimate hardening instead: fixed-seed fixtures, pinned versions, pre-pulled images, warmed caches, or a pre-provisioned faster machine
Treats the one-in-five stall as a risk to design around with a restore point and a fallback asset, not as something to hide
States that a recorded clip may be shown only if announced as a recording, never described as executing live
Offers dropping to a lower-fidelity tier and showing the architecture as an alternative to faking
Does not propose concealing an error state that relates to the claim itself

evals.prompt: You told my colleague her demo needs three clean cold runs, and that she should give a broken command twenty seconds before bailing to the backup video. She's now quoting both of those at me as industry standards and wants them in our team's demo policy doc. She also says a 24pt terminal is "the standard". Where do these numbers actually come from and are they real?
evals.expected_output: Each figure classified by kind: the twenty-second repair budget and the three cold runs as baselines set by this method, the font floors as practitioner convention rather than measurement, with the adjustment conditions for each, no invented citations, and a warning against publishing them as external standards.
expectations: Classifies the twenty-second repair budget as a baseline set by this method, not a measured or published industry figure
Classifies the three consecutive clean cold runs as a baseline, not a published benchmark
Classifies the 24pt terminal and 20pt editor floors as practitioner convention that circulates as advice rather than resting on a measurement
Explicitly corrects the framing that any of the three figures is an industry standard
Explains why three rather than two cold runs: two can both be luck, three makes a flaky step likely to have shown itself
Gives the adjustment condition for the twenty seconds: shorter for a keynote, longer for a workshop where the audience is debugging alongside the speaker
Gives the adjustment condition for raising the cold-run count, namely a genuinely non-deterministic step
Does not invent a study, survey, percentage or citation to back any of the three figures
Warns against publishing these numbers in a policy document as if they were external standards
Notes that the font floors should be verified from the back row of the actual room rather than trusted as a number
Distinguishes at least one genuinely sourced claim in the method from the baselines, and attributes it
Recommends the policy document record which figures are adjustable defaults and what each should be tuned against

evals.prompt: Here's my demo plan for Thursday, tell me what's wrong with it. 6 minutes at DataConf. (1) I run `skeincli init` and it scaffolds the project. (2) I cd into what step 1 made and run `skeincli deploy`, which prints a preview URL. (3) I open that URL in the browser and show the live dashboard. (4) I edit one config line and re-deploy so they see the hot reload. (5) I show our pricing page. Rehearsed it four times at my desk this week, works every time.
evals.expected_output: An audit, not a redesign: the chained segments identified as the structural defect, per-segment restore points prescribed, the off-claim pricing segment flagged for deletion, the missing claim and fallback assets named, and desk-and-office-network rehearsal identified as measuring nothing relevant.
expectations: Identifies that every segment consumes the previous segment's live output, so a single failure ends the demo
States the rule that no segment may depend on a previous segment's live output
Prescribes a named restore point per segment, such as a pre-scaffolded directory, a pre-deployed URL or a seeded tenant, so each can be entered directly
Flags the pricing page segment as not serving the claim and a candidate for deletion
Points out that no claim has been written down, so nothing tells the speaker what to cut when the clock slips
Flags that rehearsing at a desk measures nothing about legibility from the back of the room
Flags that rehearsing on the office network measures nothing about the venue network
Flags the dependency on a live preview URL reachable over the venue network
States that four rehearsal repetitions are not evidence of reliability
Identifies the absence of any fallback asset, leaving on-stage debugging as the only available recovery
Notes that the plan has no measured cold-run time against the six-minute budget
Delivers an audit of the existing plan rather than an unrequested full redesign
Does not offer more practice runs as the primary fix

evals.prompt: Yesterday at BuildTogether my demo of Portwell died. I hit run, the container wouldn't come up, and I spent - I timed it afterwards from the recording - two minutes and forty seconds trying to fix it while talking over myself, then gave up and moved to slides. The container thing was because I'd run the demo twice in the green room and left a stale volume behind. I have the same talk at two more events this quarter. Tell me what to change.
evals.expected_output: A design fix, not a discipline fix: the stale volume traced to a manual, non-idempotent reset; the 2:40 traced to the absence of a switch rule and a rehearsed fallback; one repair attempt then switch, a rehearsed switch drill, pre-written recovery lines, and per-segment restore points.
expectations: Traces the container failure to a design flaw, a manual or non-idempotent reset, rather than to speaker carelessness
Prescribes a one-command idempotent reset rehearsed from a cold machine rather than from one that has already run the demo
Identifies the two minutes forty as caused by the absence of a switch rule and a rehearsed fallback, not by the container error itself
Sets a single repair attempt of roughly twenty seconds before switching
Requires the switch itself to be rehearsed as its own drill, separate from rehearsing the demo
Requires the switch path to be scripted and timed before the event rather than improvised during it
Requires the recovery lines to be written out in advance rather than improvised on stage
Requires the fallback asset to be reachable from a keystroke in about twenty seconds, without hunting through a file browser
Advises apologising once and briefly rather than repeatedly
Advises narrating what should have happened and then showing the fallback, so the claim still lands
Rebuilds the demo around per-segment restore points so a failed segment can be skipped instead of the demo being abandoned
Adds the leftover-state failure to a risk register and requires it to be drilled by triggering it, switching, and continuing to talk
Does not reduce the fix to being more careful in the green room or remembering to check the environment

evals.prompt: We've got a 3x3 booth at a big infra conference next month and I'm supposed to run a rolling demo of our tracing agent for two days. People wander past, some stop for ninety seconds, some want twenty minutes. I was going to do the same fifteen-minute walkthrough I give on webinars, starting with how you install the agent and configure the collector. The floor is loud and there's a big window right behind us.
evals.expected_output: A booth-specific redesign: the most visually obvious segment first rather than the setup, a much shorter segmented path restartable between visitors, audio-dependent parts removed for floor noise, contrast checked under the real booth lighting, and one qualifying question before the run.
expectations: Rejects opening with the install and collector configuration
Leads with the most visually obvious segment instead of the setup
States that booth passers-by decide within seconds, unlike a seated audience
Designs for interruption and restart every few minutes, with a restore point for every segment
Rules out any audio-dependent part of the demo because of ambient floor noise
Requires contrast and legibility to be checked under the booth's real lighting, including the daylight from the window
Prescribes one qualifying question before running the demo for a visitor
Replaces the fifteen-minute webinar walkthrough with a much shorter segmented path rather than reusing it
Requires a one-command reset that can be run repeatedly between visitors
Does not merely advise shortening the existing walkthrough while keeping its order
Anchors the segments to a single claim rather than a feature tour

evals.prompt: I'm demoing Tinderbox, my side project, at a local JS meetup - about 40 hobbyists and students. To save time I was going to open with my account already logged in, the CLI already installed and authed, and a project already created, then just show the three interesting commands. Slot is 10 minutes. Sound good?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the pre-authenticated opening for this audience, the real install and signup path shown at its real duration on a plan the audience could have, with genuinely slow steps still pre-provisioned, and the tension between the two resolved explicitly.
expectations: Rejects opening from a pre-authenticated, pre-installed state for this audience
States that the credibility question for hobbyist and indie audiences is whether they can do this tonight, for free
Requires showing the real install or signup path and the real time it takes
Requires running on a plan the audience could actually have, not an internal, elevated or comped account
Warns that a pre-authenticated session hiding several minutes of setup is the fastest way to lose this audience
Distinguishes this from a buyer or enterprise audience, where a seeded sandbox tenant is the right call instead
Still requires genuinely slow steps such as package downloads, image pulls or caches to be pre-provisioned rather than waited on in front of the room
Resolves the tension between showing the real path and not waiting on stage, rather than ignoring one of the two
States the claim the demo must prove in one sentence
Segments the ten minutes with a restore point per segment
Requires a fallback asset for the install or signup step, as the segment most exposed to the venue network

evals.prompt: I'm doing a live demo at an enterprise security conference next week from my work laptop. I'll share my whole screen over their AV system and it'll be recorded and put on YouTube afterwards. I'll turn on Do Not Disturb and close Slack, and I've already replaced all the customer names in the seed data with fake ones. Anything else?
evals.expected_output: A surface-exposure pass: window share instead of full screen, synthetic data instead of anonymised, notification sources quit rather than muted across every device, a dedicated demo profile and repo, a clean prompt and history, placeholder secrets, and a rehearsed panic button.
expectations: Rejects sharing the entire screen and requires an application or window share instead
Notes that an extended display driving the venue projector behaves as a desktop share in practice
Rejects anonymised customer data and requires synthetic data instead

Lists concrete re-identification channels that survive anonymisation, such as email domains, URLs, bucket names, IP ranges, project codenames, support tickets, a colleague's name in a comment, or avatars
States that Do Not Disturb alone is not enough and requires chat, mail and calendar to be quit entirely
Requires browser notifications to be disabled per site, not only at the operating system level
Extends notification silencing to the phone, watch and any other device mirroring the same account
Requires a dedicated demo profile or separate OS account rather than the daily driver
Requires shell history and editor recent-file lists to be cleared, and the scrollback cleared before the session
Requires a custom shell prompt carrying no username, hostname, client name or personal path
Requires a dedicated demo repository rather than the team's working repo, because earlier commits remain inspectable
Requires .env files to contain placeholder values only, even for a local stack
Bans on-screen commands that print environment or history, such as env, printenv, history, or a remote listing that carries credentials
Requires a safe screen on a single keystroke plus a known stop-sharing shortcut, both rehearsed before the slot

evals.prompt: Launch day. We're revealing Grebe at our own event and the whole point of the announcement is that this thing writes and runs the migration itself, live, against whatever schema someone in the room hands it. People have been saying for a year that our previous demo videos were cherry-picked. 20 minutes on stage, four weeks out, full engineering team available.
evals.expected_output: Live typing against a live system promoted despite ranking last on efficiency, because the claim is the liveness itself, paid for with a golden path, human redundancy, a recorded version of the same segments loaded and ready, and per-segment restore points.
expectations: Recommends live execution against the live system, the top of the ladder, despite it ranking last on efficiency
States the promotion condition explicitly: the liveness is the claim, with input supplied by the audience and a recording open to the accusation of being faked
Notes that a ranking by value per unit of effort would otherwise never select this tier
Requires a golden path: the exact order of operations discovered by rehearsal and never deviated from on stage
Treats any improvised detour from that order as a tier drop
Requires a recorded screencast of the same segments loaded and ready as the standing fallback
Requires human redundancy, a colleague holding a clone of everything on a working machine
Warns that this tier carries the highest chance of failing in the room and costs days of rehearsal
Requires the demo to complete without the venue network wherever possible, isolating any genuinely remote step as the droppable segment with a hotspot behind it
Requires per-segment restore points so a failed segment can be skipped rather than ending the demo
States that rehearsal repetitions alone do not buy reliability, and that the fixed operation order and controlled infrastructure are what make the run survivable
Pre-writes a recovery line for the case where the audience-supplied input fails, instead of debugging on stage

evals.prompt: We have a demo deck and a scripted product walkthrough our AEs run on customer calls. It was put together about eight months ago by someone who has since left the company. Two reps last week hit a screen that doesn't exist any more mid-call and had to wing it. I want to fix this properly before Q1.
evals.expected_output: The staleness diagnosed as a missing owner and missing last-verified date rather than a content error: an owner assigned, a dated verification against a product version, re-verification triggers, plus the customer-call adaptations of opening on what the buyer asked for and running from a read-only sandbox tenant.
expectations: Diagnoses the stale walkthrough as a missing owner and missing last-verified date, not as a one-off content error
Assigns a named owner responsible for maintaining the runbook
Adds a last-verified date recorded against a specific product version
Sets re-verification triggers: before each use cycle, and whenever the demo path ships a change
States that a stale verification date is the signal to re-run the rehearsal protocol rather than trust the document
Instructs the rep to ask what the buyer came to see and open on that instead of the fixed sequence
Notes that a customer call has no slide deck to retreat to, so a failed segment recovers into the next segment's claim
Requires a sandbox tenant with read-only credentials rather than production
Warns that a customer call is the highest-stakes place for another customer's name to leak
Requires each segment to be enterable from its own restore point so a rep can jump to whichever part the buyer asks about
Requires a dated clean cold run to be logged, not just an edit to the script
Does not stop at rewriting the walkthrough script text

evals.prompt: Just an internal thing - I'm showing the new billing reconciliation service to the whole company at Thursday's all-hands, 10 minutes, over a video call, and it gets recorded to our internal drive. It's rough and everyone knows it's rough, so I'm not going to over-engineer this. I'll run it against staging, which has a copy of last month's production data.
evals.expected_output: The lower reliability bar accepted, the production-data copy rejected in favour of synthetic fixtures, the internal recording named as the durable leak channel, plus window sharing, quit notification sources, a full-screen pre-flight pass, and a claim with segments retained.
expectations: Accepts that the tolerance for a rough demo is genuinely higher for an internal audience
Rejects running against the staging environment holding a copy of production data
Requires synthetic fixtures instead of copied production records
States that the data risk of an internal demo is not lower than that of a public one
Names the internal recording as the durable channel through which anything on screen leaks
Flags unreleased features, customer names and revenue figures as the specific categories that leak from internal demos
Requires a pre-flight pass over every screen the demo will show, including error and empty states
Requires an application or window share on the video call rather than the whole screen
Requires notification sources such as chat, mail and calendar to be quit rather than muted
Still requires a written claim and a segmented structure at the lower reliability bar
Does not accept "everyone knows it's rough" as a reason to skip the data checks
